utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We are continuing with the witness, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gavric. Could you tell me if you can hear me well today?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you well. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, when we broke off the examination, the very last thing that we spoke about was until when you were carrying out your tasks as a civilian commissioner of the military council in Odzak. You said that this was from the moment in July when you were appointed as the commissioner by the civilian-military council until March, 1993, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now let us go back to that time period and the time when you were carrying out these tasks. Yesterday we spoke about the work in relation to the supplying the town with water and people who came from Samac to carry out these tasks. You also mentioned a number of other tasks that you were in charge with. What I'm interested in now, these were tasks to do with the cleaning of the town. Can you please tell me, how was this done, the cleaning of the town, cleaning the facilities in the town? Who was doing this and who was in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the town -- no, in the town and in the companies, as I said commissioners were appointed in the town and the companies were very dirty and there was a lot of documentation that was in a mess, the civilian-military council tasked me with tidying up all the facilities of all the companies, if that is possible. Since there were no roofs that were damaged, but what needed to be done was to put new panes of glass, to pick up all the documents that were on the floor, to sort them out, put them in a cupboard of sorts, I was also tasked with cleaning the main street in Odzak. There was a lot of rubbish on the street. There were bricks, there were papers, so many people had gone through; the troops, the HVO units and of course, the evacuation by the Muslims and Croats, who were fleeing because the Republika Srpska army was advancing. So the cleaning had to be done from the hotel until the SUP building through the main street. And I said to the President that I did not have physical possibility to do this job in the time allotted, because in Odzak, there were no Serb civilians except a couple of us for the first three months. And he said that we would be assigned with a workforce the following day, that we would be given workforce from Samac. The following day, a lorry from Samac came in front of the SUP building. A driver came and his escort, and these four people working on the network water supply that I spoke about of yesterday, they got off the lorry and also - it was a long time ago I can't quite remember - but 15 to 20 women also got off the lorry. In the meantime, Savo arrived and told me, "here, this is the group for you, and you can assign them to carry out the work". He even prioritised the tasks for me. He said first the medical centre and the hospital had to be cleaned, that was the first thing, and then further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I apologise but in order to streamline your testimony in the direction of the facts that are interesting for the Trial Chamber, and I presume also for the colleagues from the Prosecution and the Defence, I will just ask you some subquestions in relation to what you have just told us about. You told us that there was a group of women there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So these women who were carrying out the work of cleaning et cetera, were they separate from the group carrying out the water network supply repairs?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely. The group that was working on the water supply network, they came with them. That's true. Every day. And returned to Samac. But they were separate, completely. And they also had a policeman who was escorting them while this other group, whether they worked as a group or five of them or six of them, each group wherever they went, they also had one civilian policeman who was providing security for their own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So the same question I asked you yesterday in relation to the men who were there on the work obligation that you spoke of yesterday, so these women who were cleaning the streets and cleaning the premises in Odzak, were they also coming to the hotel to have lunch with you, do you recall your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely. Everyone was under the work obligation, the behaviour was the same, they would come, they would be assigned their task, during the lunch which was from 1200 to 1300 hours, they would come escorted by the civilian policeman, they would come to the hotel, they would sit in the hotel, all together, we would lunch, perhaps we would have a juice, coffee, that would be normal. We had no problems. There were even joint tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the course of the day, so you said they returned together with the men who also worked on the water supply network?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not together. That would depend on where the men were. If they were any repairs to be done in the town on the network, then they would be working there, perhaps in the man holes on or the pipes. But that was happening at the same time but not together, and this group of women, if they were working on three different locations, they didn't -- they didn't come together but they would come at the same time escorted by the policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, sir, my question wasn't clear enough. What I meant was if they came together, I meant they came together in the morning, that was what my question was in relation to, so in the morning they would come in the lorry together?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So where would the lorry bring them in the morning?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And these tasks for that day, where would they be given them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the weather was good, that would happen in front of the building of the TO staff where my office was, but if it was raining, then we would go into the hallway, the corridor of the building, and I would already have a plan of assignments, who would work on what and how many of them. And then Mirko Pavic was their squad commander, would assign the policeman, and sent them to do their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify one thing fully. Did you choose who would come and do this work?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Let me tell you, this was not always the same group, always the same people. Sometimes that would depend, like these four, they came continuously and this other group of women came, they were not the same persons always. It wasn't always the same people every single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now we spoke about the work obligation, and I'd like to ask you some questions of you personally. Were you also under the work obligation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is, with the civilian-military council, with the military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So just one question that stems from your answer: Did you ever get any official document, a certificate, that this was your official work obligation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, the previous answer of the witness is somewhat unclear in my submission. He was asked: "Were you also under the work obligation," and he answered yes: "That is with the civilian-military council, with the military administration." It's not -- we've heard evidence of that very -- of that distinct organ, the civilian-military administration. You should know in my submission, whether or not this witness was working for them or whether it was his assignment to simply work as one of the commissioners in turn for the civilian-military administration and who gave him that particular work assignment as well for that evidence to be -- to make any sense to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And that was precisely my next question because I believe my colleague is looking a bit forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. You answered that you were also under the work obligation. Can you please tell me, since you also said --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, just a moment. I didn't hear the beginning of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will repeat. You have now told us that you were under the work obligation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who was the person assigning the work obligation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The work obligation was determined by the military administration and the civilian council in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But for you, for you specifically, you said that you were given an official document, a certificate; is that correct, a decision?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who issued that document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given that by the president of the military council, that was the title was the Ministry of Defence, Samac and it was signed by the secretary of the ministry, Bozo Ninkovic and there was also the seal of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, let us clarify this, the fact who gave you this into your hands. But can you tell us what organ issued this decision, signed this decision? If I understood you correctly, this decision on sending to the work obligation as the commissioner, you were given that by the Ministry of Defence department of -- in Samac, and can you tell me about the seal and the signature again?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The seal was Ministry of Defence, Bosanski Samac, I can't remember what else. There was Republika Srpska et cetera. In any case, there was the seal of the ministry, Bosanski Samac, and it was signed by Bozo Ninkovic, and whatever, the minister or the deputy, that was the person that signed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps you know, do you have any information in relation to this, whether the other people, either commissioners or members of that civilian-military council also received such decisions, what you directly know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that all commissioners received decisions in the Odzak area, from the local commune. They all received decisions just like I did, from -- issued by the very same organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps whether the workmen in the work obligation that were coming to Odzak to work on those jobs that you described, did they also have a decision on the work obligation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I didn't ask them, but as we were chatting to each other informally when we were not working, we were talking normally, there was -- there were no restrictions, I mentioned a large person called Dasa. He said he had the decision on the work obligation but I didn't ask him what this decision was about. He just told me he had this decision about the work obligation. I don't know whether this related to Odzak. I don't have an absolutely certain information in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I was just interested in the facts. And the information that you have about that. While you were in Odzak, sir, and you were a commissioner, did you notice that either from the houses or from the companies, items were taken out, loaded on to lorries or trailers? If you have, can you tell us what you saw and what you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw on several occasions that items were loaded on all kinds of vehicles, lorries, horse-drawn cart, trailers, but I did not react to that. I wasn't checking that. That was not my responsibility. But I did see that but I don't know whether these persons had been given permission to do that or authority to give that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely my next question. Sir, if anybody wanted to take out of Odzak any item at all, could you tell me what was the procedure? You told us that there were checkpoints, you told us that there was the military administration. Can you tell us if a person wanted to take something out of Odzak, who did this person address? What was the procedure in place?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure was the following: The person interested in taking certain things out of Odzak had to fill in a form and a written request to the president of the civilian-military council, together with the listed items, or what this person needed to leave Odzak. This written request -- and of course this would have to be signed. Now, this written request would then have to be filed with the President of the military council, the president, as far as I know the rules, I wasn't present when this was happening, but the president would look into this request and these requests were either approved or not approved. If such a request was approved, then there were separate forms that would be copied, I think it would say "approval" or "permit" and then that permit would have the name of the person, the items that would be taken out of Odzak by this person, which items, the quantity thereof, and such a certificate would be signed or a permit would be signed by the president of the civilian-military council, would then seal it with a stamp, with a seal, with four Ss on which it said municipality of Samac, then that certificate, this official document, because the military administration was further away from our premises, somebody would take that to the military administration and then this person in the military administration also had to sign some -- this -- there and a person.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the official person?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the military administration would have to sign that and seal it by the seal of the military administration. There would be several copies, there would be one in the archive of the military administration, one would be would be in the civilian-military council. One, he had to give at the departure checkpoint from Odzak, wherever he was leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, could you just please slow down? Because we can't follow you enough.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So the last thing you said is that the person was supposed to leave this at the exit checkpoint so to speak from Odzak, wherever the person was going?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyone leaving Odzak, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So when leaving Odzak, you come across a checkpoint, a person arrives with goods and items which the person wants to take out of Odzak and shows the certificate. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A copy of the certificate was to be left with the shift leader at the checkpoint. It was only then that the person would be allowed past the checkpoint with the items.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What about if a person was not in possession of a certificate from the military administration, stamped by Odzak's military administration, could the person in that case have gone through the checkpoint just the same?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That person would have had to take another route, an unofficial route and possibly risk their lives on the way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Speaking of which, if I can just ask you to explain something to me briefly, the freedom of movement in the municipal territory, I'm talking about Odzak municipality. It is agreed that the whole territory was under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps but were there any minor, smaller units that were deployed in the area, and was it possible to go and how from the zone of responsibility, the area of responsibility of one unit into the area of responsibility of another different unit within the Odzak municipal territory?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Odzak municipality under military administration was divided into four areas of responsibility. Odzak was one area of responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Please just slow down.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. The town of Odzak itself, together with the village of Ada, was one area of responsibility. There was a special military command so to speak. Then the villages of Novo Selo, Gornja Dubica, as far as Prud and Donja Dubica. Zorici. As far as I know I was moving about those parts with permits. That was another area. And then there was the zone Gornja Mahala, Novi Grad, excuse me, I'm not looking at this, I keep forgetting. So that -- there was an area towards Gornji Svilaj and then the same towards Potocani because there was a different area, a separate area, Gnionica and Josava and I was in possession of a permit, I obtained it in Odzak. I had family in Trnjak and in Dubica and in Novi Grad so I would go there. Especially if I was going to stay for a while. The checkpoint that is at the command of the village of that area, I had to visit it and an authorised official would have to issue me with a permit to move about in in that area of responsibilities. When I went after my private business, I would go back to Odzak and I would have to return the permit, and I came back with another permit which I had, which was valid for the town of Odzak. It was like that for me and for all the other citizens and civilians who lived in the territory of Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, in each of the areas of responsibility of these smaller units, you needed to have a special permit issued; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes because there were combat operations going on there, so that's why the army was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we spoke about the military administration in Odzak. Can you please tell me to the best of your knowledge who introduced the military administration to Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, which we obtained from Mirko Pavic specifically and the group I found in Odzak, the military administration had been introduced by the 1st Krajina Corps whose commander was Mr. General Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you know at that time who was at the head of the military administration?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I forgot the last name but I know that he was Colonel Gojko and as far as I understood, he was the assistant of the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps for civilian affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps Vujanic was the last man of that person, the colonel?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we need to correct something in the transcript here on page 12, line 23, perhaps. I said Vujanic. V-U-J-A-N-I-C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Vujanic, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. To the best of your recollection, how long was the military administration in Odzak in place?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military administration in Odzak was there until the municipality of Odzak was established in 1994, towards the end of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like you to tell me the following, please. If you can explain, the structure of government in Odzak, what was the highest organ of authority in Odzak? Who was below that? So what was the structure under the military administration in terms of the government bodies in Odzak? How was it organised?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the military council, as the chief body, and the military administration, I mean, as the main. Then the civilian-military council and we as commissioners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You kept correcting yourself so the transcript is a bit confusing. Who is at the top?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask the witness maybe to just draw a sketch of the hierarchy in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe this will be helpful. With the assistance of the usher I could give him a blank piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll start.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I understand what you've written but for the transcript we need to clarify this. The upper most box contains the words... ?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Below that, the second box?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian-military council.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me about the third box?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commissioner for the local commune of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... As an ID document and as soon as we get the translation of this document, we will ask for full admittance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be treated as D50/ter for the B/C/S. Thank you. D50/4 ter ID. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gavric. Tell me, please, you personally, did you have certain experiences in Odzak in relation to your personal property, to your house, during your stay in Odzak as commissioner?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber about your experience?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of July, when I came to Odzak, as I've already said, on that day, I came to my own house, I put a lock on it and I closed the windows. When the civilian-military council had been set up and I had received permission to move about finally, I would visit my house practically on a daily basis, three or four times. It's near the hotel and the theatre. It's in the centre of the town. It was down at the end of a blind alley. And without going into too many details, in that period of 1992, until the month of November, my house was broken into nine times, although the first time, after I visited, after I had obtained my permission to move about, I put a sign on the door saying, "this is a Serb house, Dusan Gavric, commissioner for the local community of Odzak, please do not touch". However, it was touched, and I got really angry when I saw that. I took two Kasikara hand grenades and there were two doors into the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps this is a bit more detail than we required but your personal house, it had a sign saying, "Dusan Gavric's house, commissioner". It was broken into eight times throughout the period?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nine, nine times, altogether nine times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What did they take from the house, tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must say that there is a staircase leading up to the first floor, and they could -- they couldn't take anything down the stairs because the staircase is very narrow. They had to use the balcony and a wooden ladder to transport the items downstairs but they took everything they could, the TV set, cutlery, dishes, suits, clothes, even books, my kids' PC, the -- my wife's sewing machine. Whoever came took something away. No one went there without taking something.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, the following thing I'd like to ask you is something in connection with the position, location, of certain buildings that you referred to during your testimony. You talked about the police station. You also talked about the Odzak TO building. Are these two buildings close?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they're adjacent, on the same line, there is perhaps four or five metres between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In relation to those two buildings, how far is the hotel in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hotel is at the end of the main street, the distance is perhaps between 400 and 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You told us that you slept at the hotel for a while?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What I want to know about now is Mr. Simo Zaric's stay at the hotel, his sojourn at the hotel. The first question, did he sleep at the hotel in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes, but not very often really, because Mr. Zaric had a vehicle and a driver at his disposal who would then drive him back to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the name of Mr. Zaric's driver?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tutnjevic, Toso. I think his first name is Toso or rather they called him Toso, I don't think that's his first name. I can't think of the name right now. Tutnjevic, and his nickname is Toso.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know, perhaps, if Mr. Zaric had any office that he used at the hotel for work?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the hotel, the section of the hotel where the reception is, there was an office of officials who used to work at the hotel there, at reception, that's where the office was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, in your personal experience, what did Simo Zaric do in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said at the beginning, he was a member of the civilian-military council. However, after between ten and 15 days, that's when he -- he was assigned the office, after about 15 days. We met and he asked me the following: He said that he was doing some work in relation to military security, military security. He said he had an office at the hotel, that he was working in cooperation with the military administration, and that he had several tasks that he had to carry out in cooperation with me. Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He then asked me the following, that I should leave a list of all Serbian civilians who during the HVO were in Odzak and who were then found in Odzak. Then, that those of us from the civilian structures living in Odzak, that I should ask both the citizens who were there in Odzak, not very many, but to ask them to find any document, any piece of paper that could be found whether in around the houses or premises of the municipality or in the offices of the parties, both the SDA and the HDZ, and that all these documents, papers, should be handed to him, and the third thing he told me, he didn't go into any details but he said that he should go to Novi Grad, that he had to carry out some interviews with civilians who had come from detention, who had just been released, and that's what I know about Simo Zaric's activities in Odzak. I have to stress that all the commissioners, as far as I know, they found certain pieces of paper to do with the HVO authority that were left in a hurry and they were handed over and I don't know what Simo Zaric then did with those documents. I know that he cooperated with the security officer from the military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Simo Zaric have anything to do with the activity of the people from Samac who were brought from Samac under the work obligation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just a couple more things?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, before you leave that section I'm interested in the time period when Mr. Simo Zaric collected these papers which people picked up from the houses or the offices. What was the time period, at least the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, actually you reminded me of the question that I didn't pose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gavric, can you tell me, how long did Mr. Simo Zaric stay in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact date but I think it wasn't more than a month altogether, about 30 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if we can specify this a little, in 1992, when would that be, until what month?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably until the end of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did -- was Mr. Zaric in Odzak after that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw him again until 1996 when I moved to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you know Jelena Zaric?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber if they are related -- if she is related to Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she is his younger sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Was she in Odzak and if so, what did she do there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She was in Odzak. After the military council was established, she was working as a -- working in administration, working as a typist, the military council, I'm not quite sure how long, could be four or five months and then later on she worked at the Red Cross in Odzak. And she worked in the humanitarian aid and all the other tasks that were carried out by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, before the war, did she live in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, can you tell us, until what time did you stay in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed in Odzak until the end of December, 1995, when, after the Dayton agreement was signed, when Odzak was made part of the Federation, I moved out to the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: While you were in Odzak, were Serbs returning, those that had been detained or those who had fled, were they returning to the territory of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but as far as the Serbs who had fled to different places, relatively few people returned to Odzak, so until the end of 1992, Odzak had literally only 126 citizens. There were mostly almost 100 per cent former citizens of Odzak but in those villages of the local commune, refugees did come back, depending on where they had been, anywhere in the former Yugoslavia, or somewhere else, and then I also know that our Serbs from imprisonment came back from the territory of the municipality of Odzak, and I think that at the end of 1992, whether there were two or three exchanges that took place. I know that because the military administration organised the dinner in the hotel and there was a Buffet. People were welcomed. They had a rest. They had something to eat and then there was a bus that was brought and then they were driven to their homes, depending where they were from, Dubica, Vranjak, Novi Grad and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And refugees from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did they come to Odzak during that time period? Not people who had lived in Odzak before the war, in the municipality of Odzak but did people come from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in January 1993, there were refugees who came from the villages of Bistrica, Ljeskovica and Gostovici. These are from the municipality of Zavidovici. They came and they started living in villages that used to be Croat villages, that is Novo Selo and Dubica. Gornja Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think that we are nearing the end of the examination. I will just confer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I may consult my counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other counsel wishes to examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Miroslav Tadic's defence has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a couple of questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very brief issues, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gavric, my name is Pantelic, I have Defence counsel for Dr. Blagoje Simic. I'm just going to ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you were answering the questions of my colleague regarding the survey on the situation of the facilities in Odzak, you said that the author was Rajko Dervenic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Rajko Dervenic was from Doboj, he was from the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rajko Dervenic, until the war broke out in Odzak, in April, he was a director of the water supply company in Odzak. He then left Odzak and went to Doboj, and he worked in SUP, that is in MUP, in Doboj, on -- as an accountant, because he had economics degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And considering that he had a degree in economics, he knew about the economic capacity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Considering that Doboj is south of Doboj -- south of Odzak, does this mean that there were certain interests to do with Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, was he killed sometime in the autumn of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He was killed in Doboj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This report that he compiled, you discussed that at the council of the military administration?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. That is the report which I saw for the first time when Rajko came to the -- the late Rajko came to me, to my office to ask me informally, ask me how I was and to send me greetings from my wife who was working under the work obligation in Doboj. So among other things, he told me that he and another group of people had created, compiled this report, and he told me, "have a look at this," and to tell you the truth, I didn't look at it in the detail, I just leafed through it and as far as I was able to say, I said, "that's very well, Rajko, it seems that there is a lot that's left." And that was all our conversation. It didn't last more than five minutes. He went to a meeting of the civilian-military administration, that was held that day, also in the building of the staff of the TO, where I had my office but it was in a different part of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So he went to that meeting with the report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He went to the meeting with that report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I don't know who he handed the report to, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information -- now you just said to my colleague that nine times your house had been broken into in Odzak. Do you have any information as to who had been taking items from your house?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that these were our people, Serbs, who had done that, nothing else, I never -- I never caught any one red-handed individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, as part of the area of -- in the -- of the military administration, was military police active?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was. They were deployed at checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you file any kind of criminal report against the persons, persons unknown, who had done this to you, who had broken into your house? Did you do anything because of what had been done to your house?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. That was impossible. Not just to bring it before the council, it was impossible to control, because my -- not just my house but Odzak didn't have many citizens. It was practically out of the way, although it was in the centre of town. So it's not that any -- that burglar would have been afraid of being seen. This could have happened in the middle of the day, not just my -- this just didn't happen to my house but happened to most houses and flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you complain to anyone verbally? Did you tell anyone about this problem, anyone who was the authority in the military administration?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't see where this is taking us in relation to the defence of your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is actually my last question, just to cover the -- I would say chain of command within the military administration, who is in charge for what, including security of the persons, properties et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So simply as that, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So that's the last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's the last question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So can you just tell me this: Did you complain to anyone verbally from the military administration about the problems you had with the house?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To whom did you complain?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, now I've forgotten, he was a captain, to the captain of the military police, I complained to him and to the main security officer of the military administration, the two of them, but their reply was, oh, that would have to be -- you -- one would have to have secret agents to hide and to see who would come to that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gavric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, I hope to be brief with you this afternoon. And to help me in that task of being brief, if you can answer questions with a yes or a no, that will speed up this whole process and we can finish this hopefully quickly. You mentioned that one of the men who came to do plumbing work in Odzak was a large man with a mustache, nicknamed Dasa?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I didn't ask him about his name then even.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. If I suggested to you his name was Izet Ramusovic, would that -- would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be sure, because I really never asked his name and last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, that's fine. Okay. The municipality of Odzak, as it existed before the war, had a very sizeable population of Croats and Muslims, didn't it? Both in the town itself and in the area outlying the town but within the municipality, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were there more Croat villages than there were Serb villages in the outlying areas of the Odzak municipality?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yesterday I listed that. I'll repeat now, that there were nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's unnecessary. All I want to know, there were more Croat villages than there were Serb?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your position is that after the Serb forces had taken over Odzak, almost all of these Croats and Muslims, both from within the town of Odzak and in the outlying areas of the municipality of Odzak, had gone?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found no one there, according to the information I had obtained from a Serb woman whom I met on the first day, the 17th of July, in Odzak. That was what she told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. And is that the position from what you could see for yourself?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because I arrived, because I arrived in Odzak on the 17th of July, and I found no one there, not a soul, not a single civilian, Croat or Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That meant, didn't it, that there were substantial numbers of Croat homes and Muslim homes and Croat businesses and Muslim businesses where the owners had fled?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Savo Popovic was a member of the Crisis Staff, the Serb Crisis Staff, in Bosanski Samac, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, because I didn't go to Samac in 1992, not since new year of 1992, not a single time. Therefore I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. You may not have gone to Samac but does that mean that you didn't know, you weren't informed in some way, of his membership of the Serb Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never asked him. I don't mind other people's business, especially private business, I'm that sort every person. I never asked him about his position. All I know is that he had been into football before the war. He was a coach of a local team over there but what you're asking me about, really I don't know. I don't wish to say something here that I'm not sure about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Your appointment, short-lived as it was, as a police officer, was made by Savo Popovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. As Jerko told me, not only me but other five people -- Mirko told me, using walkie-talkie, not the phone, he talked to his own superior, Stevan Todorovic, complaining that he didn't have enough people, that there were only six of us there, and he said he had agreed with his superior that we should also come and work as police officers in Odzak pursuant to that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So Mirko Pavic assigned you and you say that he told you --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of the department, not Mirko Pavic, Mirko Pavic told me that he had obtained approval from Stevan Todorovic, his own superior, that the six of us - excuse me - should join the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did Mirko Pavic appoint or at least convey orders for the appointment of other policemen, other than the six that you have just mentioned, yourself included?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no others, at least he didn't tell me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were other policemen appointed in Odzak in the period of time throughout 1992 and early 1993?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly, as far as I know, it was the same group, maybe they were one or two changes towards the end of 1993, but it was a very small group. There were perhaps two or three people. I'm not sure, people who returned from detention and people who had been police officers before, they were detained in 1994. Well, actually 1993, thereabouts. There were changes, Mirko Pavic plus another six of them plus those five who were with me so that was in 1993, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just slow it down and you can tell me about 1992 first of all. The first group of policemen that you were aware of in Odzak in 1992 was a group appointed by Stevan Todorovic of about six?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And throughout 1992, that was about the size of the police force in Odzak, some may have come, some may have gone, but that was a sort of size of the group?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did Stevan Todorovic make further appointments to the police, throughout 1992? These few additions that were required?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did Stevan Todorovic ever visit Odzak to handle police matters?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I saw him once, but I don't know if he came or how many times he came or if he came at all. I saw him once about town. He was just walking around. I didn't even know Stevan Todorovic back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on to another topic. You agree, I think, don't you, that Odzak faced a number of infrastructure problems following the war, the battle that had taken place, and they were apparent to you when you returned to Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The problems were extensive, they included water, getting the water supply coming back on, health screening, pensions distribution, setting up stores that could sell items, setting up a green market, setting up a lavatory, the creation of schools, and what you've told us today, cleaning up the SUP, police station, and I suppose other areas of Odzak. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you would agree that these were reasonably extensive problems, they required time to fix, time for these repairs to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, quite some time actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the period of time that Mr. Zaric was in Odzak, these repairs were already underway? Repairs and projects, I should say.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't specify about the period. You're asking me about the period. That month. So if you want me to put it that way, specifically in that period, the water system was back to normal and there was a generator for electricity. That was put into function. The streets had been cleaned, and they began cleaning the buildings too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. In August of 1992, in August of 1992, these repair works and these -- these repair works and these projects were underway?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you would agree that much of the work that was being done required specialist labour as well? For example, plumbers.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: There were very few civilians in Odzak in 1992, very few civilians residing. It was mainly populated by the army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, until the end of 1992, there were only 126 civilian inhabitants, elderly people, children, a handful of us men, some women. We, the men --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And so therefore, the workers to carry out these repairs to infrastructure conduct the sort of projects that you have told us about, had to come from elsewhere, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And a good number of them came from the Samac municipality, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And most of them were of non-Serb ethnicity, most of them were Muslims and Croats, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the organ or the body or the institution that supplied these workers carrying out these repairs was the civilian administration in Bosanski Samac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it's a call for speculation. The witness clearly indicated that he was not in Bosanski Samac up until the end of 1992, so how could he answer whether what was happening in Bosanski Samac at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: He could very easily answer it. He was on the ground there. There might be all sorts of sources of information on that particular topic. He might have spoken to the civilian administrators by phone, he might have spoken to the workers. He might have seen proclamations, he might have received information on the topic in a thousand different ways. The question is perfectly proper in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the witness can answer. If he doesn't know, he can say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So the body that was supplying these workers who you have said came from Samac was the civilian administration in Samac, either the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency or later the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact body or institution who sent people from Samac under the work obligation, so the -- what follows is that I couldn't name it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. One thing is certain, and that is this: Savo Popovic was able to arrange for a supply of these non-Serb workers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savo Popovic told me that there was no problem in connection with my tasks, under my work obligation. What the minimum of people was I needed to carry out those tasks, he said he would send as many.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. So you agree with me that Savo Popovic was able to supply non-Serb workers to carry out some projects in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And these continuing requirement -- sorry, these continuing projects that you've told us about, continuing infrastructure works, required workers continuously?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you've testified today that throughout 1992, the number of civilians residing in Odzak was very small. I think you said only about 126 by the end of the year, therefore the need to bring in continuing numbers of workers remained the same throughout 1992? In fact remained the same until the area became populated, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really remember the date, specific date, when people under the work obligation stopped coming from Samac. I believe it was but I'm not sure, truth to tell, I think it was at some point during 1992, when plumbers stopped coming, because our people had returned from detention, specifically three plumbers came back, they started working in Odzak, and those from Samac stopped coming. Our own electrician came back and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just bear with me to allow me to look at my notes from today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Today you said that the workers who came from Samac to carry out work obligation changed. There were constant changes particularly to the group of women who were conducting cleaning and other tasks. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't every day. It took about seven days to memorise people's faces because I would go out and meet them in the morning and during lunch but yes, occasionally some people were changed, and different people, men or women, came, continually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who arranged for these different -- for this stream of different workers to come in and do all this work in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whose task that was. I'm not familiar with that. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did Savo Popovic say to you that he could arrange workers on only one occasion, that is in regard to the plumbers, or did he tell you, did he entertain your requests for more workers on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never requested workers outside the tasks that I was given by the military administration, by the council. Generally speaking, from the very first day, I would be given certain tasks, I'd go to the president of the military council, Savo Popovic, and I'd say, "I need ten people to carry out this tasks," for example, and he would say, "very well, you'll get the ten people you need". But I would like to emphasise that this was -- there were no great fluctuations. It was usually the same number of people, or about the same number of people. It was usually between 10 and 20 people with very few fluctuations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Who would decide which tasks had to be done?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Odzak, myself, as all the other commissioners, across the local communes, the civilian-military administration was in charge, and they were responsible to the military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So commissioners such as yourself would make an assessment of the job that needed to be done in their area, they would then go to the military administration -- civilian-military administration, explain the job that needed to be done and the civilian-military administration would arrange for the workers to do the job?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We didn't have authority to act on our own. Whatever the military administration considered necessary, what they thought needed doing, I told you that was the task of the military-civilian council and I tried to carry out such tasks in the best way possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I believe that the answer of the witness was not properly recorded. He said actually, what the military administration considered necessary, they would forward these to the military-civilian council and then they would forward it to us as commissioners. That was actually what I heard, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So the top body in the municipality of Odzak, the military administration, or military -- the military would decide what jobs had to be done, having made a decision, they would in turn go to this civilian-military administration, and the civilian-military administration would in turn distribute the tasks to various commissioners such as yourself?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Are you aware of other commissioners such as yourself going to the civilian-military administration and seeking workers to carry out tasks?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Are you aware of other members of the civilian-military administration, apart from Savo Popovic, organising workers to carry out tasks?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Approximately how many members were there on the civilian-military administration? Apart from Savo Popovic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, to the best of my recollection, 11, a total of 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: One of whom was Simo Zaric, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Zaric, for the first ten or 15 days, before he started working on security tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Let's get this clear. Simo Zaric was on the civilian-military administration, correct, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian-military council, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Simo Zaric worked on this civilian-military council, assisting it, for a period of ten or 15 days? And that was before -- before he started security tasks?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And Simo Zaric was doing his level best, wasn't he, to restore civilian life, to contribute to the repairs of the infrastructure of Odzak, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think Simo had no tasks related to that, as far as I know, from my personal experience. He was not involved with that. It was up to Savo Popovic, the president of the civilian-military council only.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What was he doing for the first ten or 15 days before he transferred to attending to security tasks?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth to tell, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: However, you are clear and certain that he was there for ten or 15 days, that he was not engaged in security tasks and during that ten or 15 days, he was on the military-civilian council?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, Simo Zaric spent a total of about 30 days in Odzak. Between ten and 15 days -- He didn't stay long as security officer. So half the time he was on the military council and the remaining part of the time he spent in Odzak he worked on security-related tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And he was a high-ranking official, wasn't he, in the civilian-military council in Odzak because he was the deputy, wasn't he, to Savo Popovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was not Savo Popovic's deputy. He was only a member of the civilian-military council to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any meetings of the civilian-military council in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the first meeting, when all the commissioners were in attendance, all the commissioners of the local commune, only the first meeting, we were there, and after that we no longer took part in the work of the civilian-military council, but rather commissioners would be given tasks from the president of the civilian-military council in their respective local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. So the military-civilian council held an initial meeting, and present were Savo Popovic and Mr. Simo Zaric and other members of the civilian-military council?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In addition to the members of the civilian-military council at this meeting, you and other commissioners attended, to be briefed on your tasks and how to go about your job?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, in principle, we were given tasks, but then the president of the civilian-military council said that he would talk individually to each of the commissioners of the local commune and give them their tasks. That he would go to each of these villages and give them tasks, every commissioner would be talked to individually, at the local commune where this commissioner was working, and that's -- that was the case with me, when he told me that the first task would be to carry out repairs to the water system, which I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is this an appropriate time for the break, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will continue our proceedings at 1615 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, after this first meeting that you've told us about, of the civilian-military council at which Savo Popovic and Simo Zaric were present, did you attend any other meetings of that body?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And please be close to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't realise I was distant from it. I will adjust.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You've told us that you went to a meeting of the civilian-military council and present were Savo Popovic and Mr. Simo Zaric. Apart from that --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment ago I told you when you asked me, when I said that we were at the first meeting, all of us commissioners of the local communes, which was attended by all of the members of the civilian-military council, headed by Mr. Savo Popovic, and among other people, members of the civilian-military council, there was also Mr. Simo Zaric who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Now apart -- apart from that meeting, did you go to any other meetings of the civilian-military council?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you aware of where -- of how often the civilian-military council met, how often they convened?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it happens, I know that because I lived and worked in Odzak, because my office was on the second floor and they were on the first floor, and so when I saw that they were all gathering there, I assumed that the meeting was going to be held, of the council, and this -- that happened at least once a week, as far as I can recall, although I didn't attend the meetings, I wasn't involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know if Mr. Simo Zaric attended these weekly meetings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to remember now. If you're insisting on how many meetings he was, I don't know how many meetings there were, from the very first meeting, and then for a fortnight, whether there were three, four or six, and I cannot tell you exactly. I know he attended the first meeting but whether he also attended all the time all the others, I don't know, I can't tell you because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll move on to another topic. You supervised the four Muslim men who repaired the waterworks?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Myself and the policeman who was providing security.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to supervising that particular job, did you supervise other jobs?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were jobs for the other part of the work obligation, the one that I mentioned, which was to clean the buildings of the hospital, and then the administration buildings of all the companies, sorting out the archive files and all the other jobs, so I oversaw these jobs as well, together with the policeman who wasn't supervising but he was providing security, physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you and this policeman who was supervising, was he one of Todorovic's policemen from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with the question in respect to Mr. Todorovic, I apologise, but the way the previous answer of the witness was that he was supervising and the policeman was providing security, and now the question was and this policeman who was supervising.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I apologise. That's not what I meant. I will change it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The policeman who was guarding or providing security, was he -- was he one of the policemen working for Todorovic from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, because there was, and this is something I mentioned earlier, the work was done in about three or four groups, of those 25 people who came for their work obligation, so each working group had their own policeman that was providing security, and it was a normal thing that among those people, there were policemen who had been -- who had come from the police station in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And one of them was a man named Stojan Blagojevic, I believe?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know who Stojan Blagojevic is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Stojan Blagojevic, I did not know him. I said that in my testimony yesterday, I didn't know him personally, until he -- he came -- he brought these four plumbers. There was a driver, he was the co-driver. It was later on from Mirko Pavic that I heard that this man was called Stojan Blagojevic and that he was responsible for these four men being brought from Samac to Odzak. That's what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So he was the escort who accompanied them from Bosanski Samac to Odzak to carry out their work assignment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All of the projects that you conducted, were they all conducted in the Odzak area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part of the work obligation from Samac that was given to me to be carried out, apart from the cases when there was one intervention that I spoke about yesterday, at the cattle farm yesterday, in Novi Grad, when Dasa went with the policeman, the other interventions, the working group that worked in Odzak did not go outside Odzak. I don't know whether there was a group from Samac that came and went to other locations. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You experienced -- let me withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours just bear with me while I look at my material, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, Mr. Zaric was interviewed on the 2nd of April, 1998 by officers of the Office of the Prosecutor, Defence counsel will find this at page 95 of P141 ter. And the officer who interviewed him asked him this question: We've heard that a number of non-Serbs from Samac municipality had to go to Odzak to do different types of forced labour. Were you involved in any of that activity, forced labour activity? And

utterances.speaker: MR. ZARIC REPLIED
utterances.text: I know it took place. I was not involved. This kind of mandatory labour was also obvious in Samac, and they were mainly related to the non-Serbian population. My wife Fatima received a call-up paper that she had to clean the streets. Of course, it isn't a problem, management of labour isn't a problem if you distribute them among everybody who is not involved. But it was only to do with the discrimination of non-Serbian population that were forced to clean the streets or carry out heavy manual labour. Decision for that was made by the Secretariat for National Defence and that man in charge was Bozo Ninkovic, a member of the Crisis Staff and somebody who had influence over that problem. Now, do you agree with Mr. Zaric's assessment that forced labour took place in Odzak, just as it did in Samac?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how this forced labour was organised in Samac, but the fact is that the work obligation group that came from Samac to work in Odzak, starting from the plumbers and then this group that came to clean, they worked the work hours from 8.00 to 1600 hours in the afternoon. They had a break for lunch that I told you about. They ate lunch together with us at the hotel. None of us, specifically myself, we never forced them to work, to, as we say, really break their backs working. It was never said, "today, five offices have to be finished." And the same thing went for the plumbers as well. They did work in Odzak, but they were not forced to work until they were exhausted. They were working as if there was no war, but everything else, as to who was sending them and as regards with that unfortunate war, well, I really don't know what was going on in Samac. I'm telling you about Odzak, and I guarantee, I guarantee, I put my life on what I -- what happened in Odzak. I told you all about it, what was happening in Odzak is that the first day they were given policemen to provide security for them, for their own personal physical safety, because nothing could happen to them in Odzak while I was there, while I was working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gavric. However, I'm not seeking a description of the working day of these people. I merely ask you this: Mr. Simo Zaric has described this sort of work in Odzak and in Samac as forced labour. Do you have any reason to disagree with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was reading this portion of Mr. Zaric's interview and I never seen these words being used, that "forced labour". It was working obligation, the words that were used. And I believe that we have one slight problem. My colleague, when he reads in English, and since I believe that the interpreters don't have before them this particular document, so that what we received is not actually what is in B/C/S in the document, so in order to facilitate all this, maybe the document could be shown to the witness and read it instead of receiving a translation that is not 100 per cent accurate with the one that we have in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I rely on the translations that I get, if Your Honours please, the words that I've seen in the question were -- "had to go to Odzak to do different types of forced labour, forced labour activity" in the question, then in the answer, "mandatory labour".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The question contained the term "forced labour," and then in the answer, it's "mandatory labour".

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mandatory labour it strikes me he's talking about forced labour and refers to the discriminatory aspect in his answer. I was going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because the other problem with that is we have the other term, work obligation which would appear to be nearer to mandatory labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't speak B/C/S I use what material I have before me and this is the answer I have translated. I'm happy, I think it's only fair, that the witness be shown the actual text of Mr. Zaric's answer, and perhaps he can read it out and any problems with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but the other point I was looking at the answers of this witness, and his explanations, he wouldn't be the one who would be able to conclude whether that was forced labour. He has explained how these people were working, the hours and how they were having lunch together. That's all he can say. The conclusion that that was forced labout, I don't think it's up to this witness to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well, You Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let me move on to another topic. You've told us that following the departure of Serb forces -- sorry, following the arrival of Serb forces, the Croat and Muslim population largely disappeared from Odzak, and that they left their homes and businesses. Was property collected --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
