utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object. So far, the witness said that the population of Odzak, Croats and Muslims, left before the arrival of Serb forces, not after the arrival. And I think that this is confusing to the -- for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The point is taken and Mr. Krgovic is correct. That's a mistake on my part. I'll rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You've told us that Croat and Muslims -- Croats and Muslims largely left the province -- the municipality of Odzak prior to the arrival of Serb forces, and that that left homes and businesses unoccupied. Was the property that was left behind by those Croats and Muslims collected in any sort of organised fashion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, no. I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you ever see groups of labourers from Samac collecting possessions from Croat homes or Croat businesses or Muslim homes and Muslim businesses?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that in Odzak. Perhaps -- no, no. This is in relation to people in Samac. Perhaps it happened but no, no, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry, would Your Honours just bear with me? I think I can speed up my cross-examination if you just give me a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You've said that you were shown a list of factories and property in those factories by your friend very soon after your arrival in Odzak. He showed you the document that he had prepared. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And do you know on whose instructions he prepared that list and that document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know who told him to carry out that survey and prepare that document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, he didn't tell me, nor did I ask him that. As it happens, what happened, happened so I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric was also interviewed on the 3rd of June, 1998, by -- again by officers of the Office of the Prosecutor. For the purposes of Defence counsel they will find this at P142 ter, B/C/S at page 137, English at page 138. And he was describing events in Odzak just after the takeover by Serb forces, and said that when he arrived in Odzak, much material had been taken by Croatian forces but a lot still remained in factories and that a commission, as part of the military council, went from company to company and wrote down the machines, what was there in terms of finished products, what state it was in, how much wheat or corn there was, how many domestic animals, and the military council wrote all this down and through Commander Popovic transferred it to the Crisis Staff in Samac. Now, do you have any idea what Mr. Zaric was talking about when he said that? Are you aware of what phenomenon, events, he was describing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about these events and I don't know when that happened. If that happened at the first meeting and the subsequent meetings that I did not attend, then I did not attend the meeting at which Mr. Zaric was talking about, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did your friend who provided you with the document, the list - and for the purposes of the record I'm speaking of D49/4 - tell you that in addition to factories, he or his associates had conducted a survey of crops, agricultural products, animals?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because when I was talking in relation to this, I said that we were there for a very short time, when he showed me that, we were just five minutes. First we were talking informally and then it was just coincidence that he showed me this document but there was nothing else in relation to this that we spoke of, not later, absolutely I even forgot about that document. We never discussed it any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And just finally, on this issue, Mr. Zaric, in the same answer, went on to say: Every day it was organised through the executive council and their institutions, they took these machines and these goods, they say that they sold them and gave up some of these goods so that the Army of Republika Srpska could be fed but I believe that a large amount went into their pockets, of which I have no physical evidence but it went that way because it was looted, and that's the way things were done during this war. Now the aspect of what he said that I'm interested in is this: Are you aware of the executive council or I should say the civilian-military administration, organising the seizure of assets, property, and transferring it to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe there is some confusion here. I believe that we have a confusion here. First of all, who Mr. Zaric was referring at, when he spoke about executive council, I mean that by now we know that there wasn't any executive council in Odzak. Whether he was referring to Bosanski Samac, that's -- maybe not up to, but Mr. Zaric will give his explanation at that point but I believe that the way the question is posed, it's very confusing for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let me ask you, are you aware of the military council recording extensive lists of property and through Commander Popovic, transferring it to the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac? Did you hear or see anything that indicated that that was occurring?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have never seen or heard anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. In the course of that interview, the interviewer asked Mr. Zaric if he had -- if he said that he had no knowledge of looting, if Mr. Zaric had no knowledge of looting, and he replied, "When I talk about this looting, I said it was done in an organised manner." And then he went on to deny personal involvement. Did you see anything that looked like organised looting to you in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you couldn't take anything out of Odzak through the checkpoints without the relevant permissions issued by the military council and the military administration, there were lorries that goods were being loaded on to, but personally I don't know whether these goods were taken to Samac or elsewhere. They were going somewhere with those items but I can't say where and it wouldn't be right for me to claim something that I'm not positive about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Fair enough, fair enough. Who was loading the lorries?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, I did not personally witness any of the loadings, nor did I personally see people load things on to the trucks. I don't know how many of them were there, nor who they were. I'm really not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Then on what do you base your assertion that you -- that trucks were loaded with goods?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you understood me correctly. What I said is that I didn't know how the goods were loaded because I thought you were speaking about heavy items. I'm not sure if you meant equipment or machinery. So you needed mechanical equipment to load that on to the trucks, and I did not see any such mechanical equipment being used. I had no opportunity to personally witness this because the companies were within the compound or perimeter. I did not go to these companies, not most of them any way, because each had their own commissioners who probably knew what was happening within the perimeter of a certain company. So the commissioners for specific companies would have known probably but I didn't know. It wasn't -- it wasn't my responsibility to know these things. It wasn't my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P103, please? Mr. Usher, may I just see the document before it's handed to the witness? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, this document is a decision to establish a committee for negotiations on territorial boundaries with Modrica and Brod municipalities, and it says that a number of men will be on this committee. One of them is Blagoje Simic. Above his name appears to be your name. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were on this committee for negotiations on territorial boundaries?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I've never laid eyes on this decision before. As far as this other thing is concerned, Samac and Brod, I know that there was a meeting in connection with that, and I attended that meeting. However, Mr. Blagoje Simic was present too. The President from Brod, from Modrica, and present too were the commissioners for the local communes, Colonel Gojko from the 1st Krajina Corps, Talic's assistant, or rather deputy for civilian affairs was present too. The meeting began in Odzak. However, at that meeting, nothing specific in relation to this was agreed. As far as I know, because later I no longer took part in any talks related to this subject, or negotiations concerning the territorial boundaries within these municipalities. I don't think there ever was an agreement on that. That's what I can tell you concerning this decision of the 16th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, when was the meeting in Odzak that you have just described or mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Odzak, this meeting in Odzak, excuse me, I remember the weather was fine, we were wearing light clothes. I don't know if it could have been November, because that's a very cold month. So I can't give you the exact month and what I said it was a very brief meeting, as far as this subject is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic was present?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What did he say and do at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Blagoje mainly -- the Colonel -- Colonel Gojko was the main speaker, not Gojkovic, Gojko. I don't know who first had the idea about the territorial division of Odzak municipality but I know that not even the Presidents of the local communes who attended the meeting were interested at that point in any kind of territorial division of Odzak municipality, and for certain parts of Odzak to be given to the municipality. This meeting took off in a tone that wasn't really serious. Not on the part of Colonel Gojko, not on the part of Mr. Blagoje, not on the part of the presidents of the local communes but rather in that group, there was a group of about ten people from Gnionica and Josava, those villages who came to that meeting on their own initiative, as far as the commissioners were concerned all the commissioners from Odzak municipality were present, and this group, to tell you the truth, worked on carrying out territorial division of Odzak and even they wanted to carve up the town of Odzak down the main street, all sort of nonsense was being said at that meeting. Eventually the meeting drew to a close and everyone dispersed and went their own way. And nothing was ever done concerning this. That's what I can tell you in connection with this specific decision. And the commission, this committee, they never met again in this composition, with these people present, apart from this one meeting. We never met again. We never talked again, not even individually, certainly not in connection with this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. Anyway, we can be clear, can't we, that the meeting was in pre-November, because it was warm weather? We can be clear that Blagoje Simic attended? And we can be clear that the army had its representatives as well at this meeting because of Colonel Gojko's presence, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And your position is that all of you men got together, had this meeting regarding the demarcation of the municipalities, but nothing ever came of it. You never had anything more to do with this topic, this group of men, or this issue.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, the document that you have before you is dated the 6th of November, 1992 and sets up this committee?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you aware of the committee having been set up even if you did nothing on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I must say that I personally don't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, my question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could it be a little -- in a different way posed to the witness? I have some doubts about --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you aware of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac -- sorry, the War Presidency of the -- of Samac municipality deciding to set up this committee, of which you were to be a member, notwithstanding the fact that you never later participated in any such committee?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who is Dragomir Tesanovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragomir Tesanovic, he hails from Novi Grad. He was the president of the SDS for Odzak municipality. He had been in detention as well as the other men from the territory of Odzak municipality. He came back from detention, I don't know when exactly he returned. At some point in 1992. And I know that he started working in Samac. Whether for the municipality or for a company, but I think it was the municipality, but I don't know what jobs and work tasks exactly. He's a mechanical engineer by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And who is Aco Minic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aco Minic was a commissioner in the village of Donja Dubica. He was a teacher by profession. He spent the whole of this time as commissioner for Donja Dubica throughout the period that I was in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you have any special qualifications regarding surveying or map reading or map making, any geographical qualifications?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The difference that Mr. Tesanovic, after the multi-party government was established, he was working for the land surveying office. He was its head. Probably Aco and I came to the group because then, in that area, the three of us were seen as the most educated people and the only people who had the same level of education in that specific period, that's as much as I can tell you right now, as I'm looking at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us about the meeting that you actually attended. Did you know what its purpose was before you went there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That there would be a meeting that day, Mr. Dragomir came and Aco too, they came together to my office, and they said -- I don't know when it was supposed to take place, whether at 10.00, they said that a meeting would be held on -- in connection with that issue, and that I too was invited, and that all commissioners were invited to the meeting. That's how it was, all the other commissioners from the local communes, that they would attend the meeting and that we would talk about the territorial division of Odzak municipality but we didn't specify, we didn't say anything about that, and nothing ever came of it, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you asked to conduct any specific tasks at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. We didn't talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you speak to Blagoje Simic regarding setting up a possible committee or -- committee to deal with negotiations on territorial boundaries?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In fact, in fact, the municipality of Odzak was divided up and the town itself subsequently became part of the municipality, the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac -- of Samac?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please have the interpretation again, slowly? The question. As far as I know, the former municipality of Odzak, that was part of the military council, was never formally or officially or unofficially divided up into these three local communes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, municipalities.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the whole thing was going on under the control of the military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How well did you know Blagoje Simic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic, I met him two or three times in 1992 or later, and even that, by pure chance, except this one meeting that we attended together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So he was not at all well known to you? He was in no way your close friend or acquaintance?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Before the war, I didn't even know who he was. I didn't know too many people in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. And he would have -- I'll withdraw that question. How well did you know Dragomir Tesanovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tesanovic, the first time I met him, unofficially, was when he took up his duty, regardless of the fact that he had been the president of the municipal board of the SDS. It was just by accident when he took up the duty of the head of the land surveyors office because I needed a document from there in relation to my property, and that was the only meeting we had before the war. During 1992, I met Tesanovic, I bumped into him several times in the street, not in relation to any meetings and then when he came back from detention, when he was having dinner at the hotel, so there are no special relations involved. We are not really friends. It's -- he's just an acquaintance in a very general sense of the word, an almost-accidental acquaintance I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You had no close working relationship with him in any way, nor a close personal friendship with him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not before the war, not during.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What about Aco Minic? How well did you know him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aco Minic, we've known each other since we were kids. He lived in Donja Dubica, he's a teacher of history and geography. I lived in Odzak myself and whenever our paths crossed, we would greet each other, we would stop to talk before the war. So it was -- we were not on visiting terms. We weren't close friends, we were acquaintances. From time to time we would sort of meet and then have a word or two, exchange pleasantries and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I take it that he didn't raise the topic with you of serving on a committee for boundaries?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Aco Minic. He didn't ever speak to you --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. As I said, he and Dragomir came to see me at the office that day in the morning and they told me there would be a meeting, and they mentioned something like I said, that I had been appointed as a member of a board. There was no decision but they said that there would be a meeting, that certain people should attend, the people I've mentioned before, from the colonel on, and that's what we talked about before the meeting. That was all we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, what board did they say that you had been appointed to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't say anything about any appointment, a board. They only said that we should attend the meeting on that day, and that's the only thing I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, the way answers were interpreted in the last one or two questions is this: You said that Dragomir came that day, told you there would be a meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, could you please approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: "Told you that there would be a meeting, and said that you had been appointed as a member of a board." They are your own words as translated. Now you say they didn't say anything about an appointment or a board. Just tell me, on the day of the meeting, did anyone tell you that you had been appointed to a board?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer this question but let me tell you first that my intention was not to deny my own words. I said that I hadn't known that I hadn't been told about the topic to be discussed at the meeting on that day, the topic. I wasn't told about the topic by either Dragomir or Aco. I think that clarifies it, and I was never shown this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. And your position is that the meeting that you attended in Odzak at which Blagoje Simic was present, neither before that meeting on that day, nor subsequently, were you ever informed of having been placed on a board to deal with boundary negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I'm wondering why you're using the word "board" when the document says committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I was using the language of the witness as it was translated to me, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: But I'm just wondering, in the B/C/S document, what word is used?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Perhaps I can -- I'll adopt the use of the word "committee" and finally wrap up the topic and be clear so the witness is clear about the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, on the day that you attended this meeting in Odzak, were you informed of being appointed to any committee to deal with territorial boundaries?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only said that there would be a meeting in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we need one small clarification of the transcript because the way the question was posed here on page 57, line 2, "your position is that the meeting that you attended in Odzak, at which Blagoje Simic was present, neither before the meeting or the day nor subsequently," all right, the question was quite long, but it was posed in a way the witness when he said no, he actually said yes, that's my position. So I would really ask kindly my colleague from the Prosecution to ask this witness short questions, if possible, to divide it in two or three questions, otherwise we receive this kind of answer which is not the actual position of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that is clarified now, the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, on the day of the meeting in Odzak, were you asked to become a member of a committee dealing with territorial boundaries?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, re-examination, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will go very briefly through this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, because my colleague from the Prosecution asked a number of questions that were in some connection with the division of the Odzak municipality, regarding certain operations and some agreements and you answered that in fact the municipality of Odzak was never divided between the three municipalities, Bosanski Samac, Modrica and I don't know which was the third one, sorry, Bosanski Brod, yes. So municipality of Odzak, the way it had been before the war, on the basis of what was it divided at the end, meaning 1995, that is in 1996? How was the line, the border line, drawn to -- for the division? Where was that agreed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps have a look at the Dayton agreement and its annexes in respect of the division of territories?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had looked at it but I didn't particularly study it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, in any case, the way that the Odzak municipality looks like now, with regard to its previous situation before the war in Bosnia, it is different, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only difference between the current situation of the municipality of Odzak and before the war is that the current situation of Odzak, the two villages Josava and Gnionica do not belong to Odzak because they belong to Republika Srpska and according to the Dayton agreement, it was the village of Prud that belonged to the Odzak municipality, because before it belonged to the Bosanski Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Precisely that. This is what I am interested in, this final division of the Odzak municipality, where --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, this topic wasn't raised at all. In fact the witness said that he wasn't involved in any negotiations regarding territorial boundaries. He doesn't know anything about the document. He wasn't involved. This whole issue of subsequent divisions of municipalities under the Dayton agreement didn't arise at all, in fact the very topic of how any division of municipalities might have occurred didn't arise because the witness didn't know anything about it. All he said is he went to this meeting and that was the end of the matter as far as he was concerned. So there was hardly anything regarding territorial boundaries that needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I will withdraw this topic. I don't intend to go deeper into it. We have some much more evidence with other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you were asked by the Prosecutor a question in relation to Stojan Blagojevic, and you replied that he had brought these plumbers that you talked about. On that occasion, did he also bring all the other workmen that were brought in that lorry or happened to be in that lorry?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just a couple more things. You spoke of and there were a number of questions by the Prosecutor in relation to the civilian-military council in relation to Mr. Savo Popovic, Simo Zaric, the membership and everything else. Now, what I'd like to just clarify or have clarified, both your answers and the entire situation regarding the -- this council, first of all you told us the civilian-military council had 11 members; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The president of the civilian-military council was Mr. Savo Popovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The other members of the civilian-military council, each member, had a task, a function, within that council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you in relation to Mr. Mihajlo Milosevic, he was an assistant to Mr. Savo Popovic for the farm?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, he was assistant for agriculture; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, the answer are being placed fairly and squarely in the witness's mouth. This is more cross-examination rather than re-examination. He's being provided the answers in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was the assistant of Mr. Savo Popovic for the economy?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was the assistant of the president of the civilian-military council, Mr. Savo Popovic, for the economy?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what I meant was economy, not agriculture.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the economy was Mihajlo Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And can you just tell me one other thing in relation to this? Who was the assistant for security?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no function like this, as far as I know. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You were asked by the Prosecutor in relation to the policemen, and those of you who were with Mr. Mirko Pavic, six of you, five of you and including yourself, those of you who have come to Odzak, and were in Odzak for a while in the police, as you've already explained. Have you -- all of you become commissioners of the civilian-military council in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just me. As it happened, just me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Will Your Honours bear with me for one second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. [Defence counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were asked by Mr. Pantelic in relation to Rajko Dervenic, do you recall? So was Rajko Dervenic a member of the civilian-military council?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And after that, did he go to Doboj?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained it. I will repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Please do, because I don't think it's very clear.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war broke out, in April, Rajko, late Mr. -- I find it very hard to talk about that -- I'm sorry. So Rajko went to Doboj, and I also said that he worked in Doboj as the head of accountancy in SUP in Doboj. After the liberation of Odzak by the Army of Republika Srpska, Rajko occasionally came to Odzak. He would carry out the task as the civilian-military council assigned him to, and the rest of the time he returned to Doboj and continued to work, to do his work as employed in the SUP, as the head of accountancy in Doboj, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You spoke about the situation that was found in Odzak, and you replied to the Prosecutor questions saying that some smaller part of things were destroyed but a lot of things were kept -- were preserved. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you came to Odzak, do you recall what was the building Hanka [phoen] looking like in the centre of Odzak, the post office, was anything burned out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was it, burned?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Was it burnt? Were they torched?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was -- it was in good condition, perhaps the panes of glass were broken but buildings, as buildings were fine and they were -- it was possible to live in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. During your stay in the territory of the municipality of Odzak, did you perhaps visit the villages of Trnjak, Dubica, Novi Grad?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation there like?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was terrible there. It was terrible in a sense that houses, stables, toilet, field toilets even, everything was burned, even the auxiliary buildings, the outhouses were -- everything was destroyed, torched during the HVO authority from April until 13, 14, 15 July, when Odzak was liberated, everything was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you were telling us about the population, that the population had left Odzak, and the Prosecutor asked you about your position, and asked you questions about that, and your response was that all the civilians had left Odzak except for those that you personally saw in Odzak and you also mentioned some people in the villages that you knew of. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps answer one other question? In Odzak, before the war broke out, there were three sisters of Mr. Zaric who lived in Odzak, not just one?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One was a doctor, the eldest one, one completed their higher business school, and she was working, and no, that wasn't the eldest but Jelena was working at the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the witness's last sentence.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All three of them lived in Odzak and worked in Odzak and they had flats in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you find them when you came to Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can the witness repeat the last part of the answer, please? The interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the very last answer you gave did not enter into the transcript when you were talking about -- I asked you whether you found the three sisters when you came to Odzak, and can you please finish your answer? You said no, but?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, can you please repeat the question now to me, the whole question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic even the earlier one, the earlier answer about the careers of the sisters of Mr. Zaric, that was not completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's go very slowly. I'll repeat the question and wait and you can answer after I finish the question. First of all, because your entire answer was not entered into the transcript, can you please say what did the three sisters of Mr. Zaric do in Odzak? Can do you it slowly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here it goes. Mara, the eldest sister, she worked at the SDK service. Jelena, the middle sister, she worked as an administrative assistant, as clerk, at the TO staff in Odzak. And the youngest sister was a doctor, I don't know whether she was a GP or she as a specialist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, my very last question was: When you came to Odzak, did you find them and their families there, and you said that you did not, except -- and can you please answer?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except Jelena, who was in Odzak. I found her in Odzak. And she had come from Serbia, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to their houses in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mara's and her husband's Nenad's house, it was a new house, it was a completely torched, there were just walls that were left. And Jelena, and the youngest sister, they had flats, and the flats had suffered the same fate as all the other flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gavric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now I really don't have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gavric, I just have two very short questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The first question is whether you heard from the plumbers who came to Odzak, including perhaps the one nicknamed Dasa, whether you heard from them about dismantling of radiators and other central heating equipment and transportation of it from Odzak to Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Really, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And my second question also relates to your conversations with the plumbers, again perhaps including the one nicknamed Dasa, and I'm wondering whether you know whether any of them worked on a house in the vicinity of Odzak, I believe owned by a film star or some other type of media personality, and whether they went there and worked on the swimming pool?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gavric, for giving evidence. We are now finished. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And Your Honours, in the meantime I have one copy of 92 bis statement. Maybe I can tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: They just forwarded me from the Registry during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is the statement of Ms. Andric, Belka, and I have B/C/S and English version, accordingly. And Mr. Usher is here, yes. Three copies for the Trial Chamber and one for the Registry and one for the Court officer to go to file. And also, Your Honour, I was informed that in a day or two, I will collect the rest of the statements so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will submit them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement will be treated as document D171/1 ter ID and D171/1 ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, the counsel? Mr. Pisarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tutnjevic.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We have already discussed technical matters, so that this can function well, and I just want to warn you again that you always wait a little while after I have asked you the question, and then answer the question, because our purpose is that your whole testimony should be properly recorded. If you have any problems, if you can't hear me, or if you cannot understand something, please stop me and ask, and let me know that something isn't working well. Have you understood this?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, for the record, can you please tell us your name and surname?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Teodor Tutnjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any other name, or as we say it, nickname?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: People call me Toso.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 28th of April, 1937.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Tisini near Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is that in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I live in Bosanski Samac, Cara Dusana Street [phoen] Number 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where did you complete your primary school?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: In Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And on the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about your educational background and what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I have completed a vocational course for a car mechanic. That is my occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what work did you do throughout your career?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Because there was no good driving service in Samac, I started working as a driver, and I have been working as a driver in Samac until I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When and where?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I served in the JNA from the 27th of July, 1958, until the 12th of July, 1960. I served in Belgrade. I was a member of Tito's guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after you have served your military service in Yugoslav People's Army, did you have any kind of rank as a reserve CO or NCO?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I left the army as a private. I have no rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, were you a member of the communist league of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me from when and until when were you a member of the communist league?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the communist league from the 29th of September, 1959, until it ceased to exist, until it stopped existing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you now a member of any political party in Republika Srpska, that is in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which one?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: The Socialist Party of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, are you married?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now we will talk about the life of citizens in the municipality of Bosanski Samac and in the town of Bosanski Samac during the time period from 1991 until the beginning of 1992. That is, more precisely, until the 17th of April, 1992. Can you please tell me, when was it that you as a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and inhabitant of the town of Samac and municipality of Samac, when did you notice that there was a disruption of interethnic relations among the ethnicities that lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, municipality of Bosanski Samac, and in the town of Bosanski Samac itself?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: The disruption of interethnic relations started immediately after the elections in 1990. It was noticeable that interethnic relations had been disrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, if I may say so, we've heard sufficient evidence on the build up of tensions among ethnic groups, and we have also heard sufficient evidence of those incidents, Valentino, and the other one concerning members of the 4th Detachment. I don't think it's necessary for to you repeat that. If you may move on, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It looks as if it's time for a break now, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will have a break and continue at 1805.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we continue, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tutnjevic, tell me, please, were you a member of the 4th Detachment of the JNA, which was part of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Briefly, please, tell us how you became a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: One day I received a call-up from the Ministry of Defence and they told me that I had been assigned as a military conscript to the 4th Detachment and that's how I became a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you report?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I reported to the command of the 4th Detachment at the Tekstilac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: By Tekstilac, you mean the SIT building?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the SIT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When did you report there or rather when you reported, what sort of assignment were you given in the 4th Detachment? Did you become --

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I got an assignment. They told me I would be the commander of a department -- of a squad, and they told -- I had ten soldiers in my squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the company?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: That was the 1st Company, the 4th squad, the 4th platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to any military drills as a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, once.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where did this military drill take place?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Near Brcko. It's a shooting range, a military shooting range. What was the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't really matter, but was it Potocari by any chance?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you do at that drill?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: We signed for weapons, we learned how to use those weapons and we got the proper equipment, and we did some target practice with real bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you perhaps given uniforms?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell us what sort of a uniform was that?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: It was a JNA uniform, olive-drab.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What sort of weapon did you sign for at that military drill?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: An automatic rifle, and an RAP. RAP, that's the combat set, with four sets, and the cleaning tools.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign a receipt for that or anything?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I signed a receipt, and I got a certificate that I was allowed to carry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This military equipment, this rifle, the uniform, where did you keep those?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I took the weapons and the uniform to my house and I kept them at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, could the witness please define RAP? He said a combat set. Could he define that a little better because I know when we look back at the transcript we won't understand what that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Pisarevic will lead him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tutnjevic, you used the expression, RAP. It's an abbreviation, can you please explain what that entailed, what the abbreviation means?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: The abbreviation means combat set or rather war equipment. It's a small bag with four magazines full of bullets for the automatic rifle and there is a small can with oil in it and a length of wire that we have a special name for, there is also a small brush for cleaning the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the 4th Detachment, did you have to request approval from the command of the 4th Detachment in case you wanted to travel or be absent for a while?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Until what happened in Samac happened, I went about my work as usual. I travel, I'd work at the company, I did not have to request any documents from the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Which means you did not have to apply for any permits or you did not inform anyone?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not need to inform anyone, nor did I have to apply for any permits because I needed none. I lived my life as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: It means that in your life, in your work, nothing changed?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Because you were a member of the 4th Detachment, did you receive any remuneration or salary for that?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not receive any kind of salary. I was on the pay list in my company where I did my daily job, and that's where I got my salary but I got no money whatsoever or remuneration or compensation from the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know whether any member of the 4th Detachment got any kind of salary or compensation for being a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that anyone got any compensation or salary for that, because most of those people who were members were working in their own companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Which was your company? Can you tell us that, please?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I was gainfully employed at the customs office, the customs zone company in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were there any meetings attended by members of the 4th Detachment? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that there were two meetings of the 4th Detachment. I attended those meetings. I don't know if any other meetings were held but I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall where the first meeting was held of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: The first meeting of the 4th Detachment was held at the memorial centre, the Mitar Trifunovic memorial centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: That's in the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who addressed the members of the 4th Detachment, who spoke at the meeting, at the Mitar Trifunovic memorial centre?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: The first speaker was Mr. Nikolic from Pelagicevo. I think he was the commander of the 17th Tactical Group. I believe Mr. Jovo Savic spoke too. Mr. Simo Zaric spoke. No, no, it wasn't Jovo Savic, it was Radovan Antic, as commander of the 4th Detachment and Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did they tell the members of the 4th Detachment that meeting? What were the aims and tasks of the JNA and by virtue of the same fact also the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic spoke about the situation in the JNA. He spoke about the political and security aspects of the situation in general. He told us that we should remain unified, that we should prevent war from spilling over from Croatia into Bosnia and Herzegovina. He talked about preventing interethnic strife. That's to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please remember what Mr. Simo Zaric spoke about?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simo Zaric spoke roughly along the same lines except he applied this to the municipal level. He wasn't talking about the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the JNA. He spoke about the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The second meeting, where was it held?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: It was held at the SIT building, the Tekstilac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who spoke at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic was not there. Mr. Radovan Antic spoke. Mr. Simo Zaric spoke. And I'm not sure if there was anyone else who spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, this concerns the 4th Detachment, what was the composition, what was the makeup, the ethnic makeup of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment included Serbs, Croats, Muslims. There were members of other ethnic minorities in it, Montenegrins, Turks, because there are several Turkish families in the Samac area. That was the makeup of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll move on to events following the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992. What do you know about events in the town of Bosanski Samac between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992, please? Tell us what you saw then, what you experienced.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th, I went to work, as usual. I was travelling that day. I took the director to the Chamber of Commerce in Doboj. He stayed at the Chamber of Commerce for quite a while and we only drove back in the evening. I drove him home and the usual way for me to do it was when I returned home, when I spend the whole day away, I would take the -- I would take the car late in the evening and drive straight to my house and then I took the car and went to my house. I went to bed. I got up the usual time the next day and I went to work. I came to where I worked, my company. There was no janitor at the door, which did not strike me as unusual because that was not the first time the janitor wasn't there. Then I reached the admin building and the door had been broken down. I entered the building and all the offices had been opened, drawers had been taken out of desks and tables, and documents had obviously been tampered with. I realised that something was happening or rather that something had happened, the phone lines were torn out of the wall and thrown all over the place, scattered. Then I went to see the director at his home. I came there, I told him that I'd been to the company building and I told him that it was chaos, and he said, "I know exactly what was happening in Samac during the night. Go home and don't leave home."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that there was some misinterpretation of the witness's words. Here it says, in the transcript, page 77, line 11, that his managing director actually told him, "I know exactly what was happening in Samac during the night. Go home and don't leave home." And this is not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can go over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The director, the manager, did he tell you that he knew exactly what had happened or that he merely say that something happened?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: He told me, Toso, I know something happened, go home and don't leave home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we please locate where exactly is your company?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: It's on the outskirts of Samac, close to the River Sava.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [no interpretation]

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: [no interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [no interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We have no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you ask the question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We have some technical problems so I'll repeat the question. Can you please tell us the location of your company?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: My company, the customs zone, is on the outskirts of Samac close to the River Sava, between the bridge on the River Sava and the port on the River Sava.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So you came home and what happened after that? Did anyone call you on the phone?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I came home and someone from the command or rather commander Radovan Antic called me and he said that I should get my men together, my unit, and that we should assemble outside the command building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you do after he had called you?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I assembled the unit, but not everyone came. Only six soldiers came. And one young man told me, "Uncle Toso, I am scared," and I told him, "Don't even leave home, just stay home." And then I went with those six soldiers who came and we assembled outside the command building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What time was this when you reached the command building?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: May have been around 9.00, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You arrived outside the command at 9.00. What did you find outside the command and inside the command at the SIT building?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: When I came there, there were perhaps 40 other people there. Some were wearing uniform and some were not. We spent an hour there, waited for more people to gather, and eventually there were about 60 people. Commander Radovan Antic took us to the embankment on the right-hand river bank of the Bosna River and he had us deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you said the embankment on the left -- right-hand side of the Bosna River, you meant the protective embankment protecting the town of Samac from being flooded?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Samac, as a town, is an area prone to flooding, so there is an embankment running all around Samac protecting the town from the Sava and Bosna rivers, so that was the protective embankment that I was referring to but just next to the embankment there are private houses, family houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. You and your squad, did you occupy one section of the embankment? Did you deploy your people there? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I deployed the few soldiers that I had and I was there with them. We occupied a stretch that was perhaps between 60 and 80 metres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: We stayed until 6.00 the next morning, about 6.00 the next morning but in the evening we had been given white armbands and we put them on, those who were wearing uniforms, they put the white armbands on to their left shoulder strap and those who were not wearing uniforms put them on the left upper arm, and we were relieved by another shift at 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: 6.00 in the morning, the next morning, on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the witness please be reminded not to talk at the same time as counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the transcript, can we just state, please, that the witness indicated the left shoulder, as the place on the shoulder strap where the soldiers were wearing white armbands and he also pointed to the left upper arm where people who were not wearing uniforms put their white armbands?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Why were you given these white armbands? Why were these distributed to you?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: It was a mark of recognition, distinction. This white armband, I wore it on the aerial of my car also.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So you went back home. What happened on that day, on the 18th of April, 1992? Did you receive any calls from the command of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: That morning, I came back home and I went straight to bed. I slept until about half past 10.00, or thereabouts. I woke up between 9.00 and 10.00 in the morning and then my wife woke me up and she said that someone had called me from the command to go there immediately and to drive there, take the car. I got ready and I went straight to the command. I drove straight to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was that the same vehicle that was property of the customs zone which you as the official driver were using?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The car is owned by the company, the customs office, and it was a Chroma car, the make was Chroma. It was blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who did you meet at the command of the 4th Detachment then?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radovan Antic was at the command of the 4th Detachment. Mr. -- No, no, he wasn't. Radovan Antic was there. Jovo Savic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did the commander tell you then?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: The commander told me that -- that the vehicle has been -- had been commandeered and that the staff or rather the Ministry of Defence had commandeered the vehicle and that the vehicle would be used, that it had given to the command of the 4th Detachment and that it would be used for their needs. As I was the driver, the person who drove the vehicle, they told me that I would be the driver for the command. I answered so what about my department? My squad? And they told me to no longer worry about that, they told me from now on you would be at the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So who did you drive? Whose driver were you once you had become the driver for the command of the 4th Detachment using this Chroma, blue, commandeered vehicle?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I drove the commander, the deputy commander, most often Mr. Zaric actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where did you drive Mr. Simo Zaric most of the time?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I drove him most to Pelagicevo, to SUP, to the line, and around the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You just said that you took Mr. Zaric to the SUP, to the police station, in Samac. So can you tell us, when you brought Mr. Zaric to the police station, did you go in with Mr. Zaric into the building of the police station?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not enter the police station with Mr. Zaric but occasionally I would enter it after him, alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zaric tell you why he's going to the police station, why you're driving him to the police station?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: He told me that he was going to the police in order to take statements, and then he would then process these statements, compile them. I don't know what he was doing. But in any case, at least what he told me, he was interested in the gathering of weapons -- in the arming, how the weapons were acquired, how they were shared out and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How long would Mr. Zaric normally stay at the police station?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: That varied, from ten minutes to one and a half hours, two hours maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you take Mr. Zaric to the police station on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not. Not on a daily basis. He did not go every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever, together with Mr. Zaric, go into the police at night in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: We were never in the SUP at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever, or Mr. Zaric, see Mr. Sulejman Tihic in the police station?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I have never seen him in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that last question is confusing. Did you ever or Mr. Zaric, see Sulejman Tihic. He can answer whether he saw Zaric and Sulejman Tihic together, whether he saw Sulejman Tihic but I think they are also asking whether Zaric saw Sulejman Tihic. It's just not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because it wasn't properly translated. Mr. Pisarevic will rephrase this in a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic, you can go over that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic just suggested this but we can clear this up. Did you ever, and Mr. Zaric together, see in the police station Mr. Sulejman Tihic?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not. Mr. Simo Zaric and myself were never in the SUP together.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Tihic in the police station?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Zaric tell you anything about what happened in the police station when the statement was taken by Mr. Zaric from Mr. Sulejman Tihic?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: On that day, when I took Mr. Zaric to the SUP, I stopped for a while, parked the car in front of the SUP, and usually there would be a person there and I would stay in front of the SUP. When Mr. Zaric left the SUP [Realtime transcript read in error "shup"] building I went into the car and he came in and he put his head in his hands and he said, "Oh, my God, Toso, what shall I do?" That's how he put it. So I asked him what happened. He said when I went to see Stiv [Realtime transcript read in error "stiff"], somebody had called him to see Stiv and then somebody had beaten Sulejman up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for this transcript to make sense, there are a few corrections in this answer. It's not what the witness said but first here on the -- on page 83, line 23, it is SUP building, not s-h-w-p, like it is here, and then on page 84, line 1, it was "Stiv," referring to Stevan Todorovic, not "stiff".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did Mr. Zaric look like to you when he was telling you these things?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: He was upset. And one could tell by looking at him that he was disappointed. He was upset, because he was shouting, he was speaking in a raised tone of voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of the fact that in the TO building, a murder was committed of a person, and how did you find out about that fact?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: Also one day, I took -- I drove Mr. Zaric to the SUP, and I was there in front of the SUP, and when Zaric left the SUP after a while, I think he stayed perhaps an hour, just over an hour. He left, he got into the car, and then Mr. Zaric told me, "Imagine, Toso, that fool killed a man." So I said, "Which fool?" And he said Lugar. And I said, "Who did he kill?" And he said Dikan, and I never thought that I had heard a shot because shots were a normal occurrence, that's how I found out that from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you find out that Mr. Zaric, together with Mr. Nikolic, Captain Petrovic, Makso Simeunovic managed to transfer the imprisoned Muslims and Croats from the TO staff to the garrison in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: One morning, when I came to the command, Zaric told me, "Toso, we are going to Brcko." Considering that he told me many things, then I said, "what are we going to do in Brcko?" So we went into the car and we set off, and then he told me, "last night I moved those from the TO to the Brcko at the garrison, at the barracks in Brcko. Those people who were imprisoned." So I said, "why did you do that?" So he said, so that they would get away from being mistreated, beaten up, and there was shelling that had increased and the roof structure was poor and this was for their own safety. So that is when I -- that was when I took him to Brcko, drove him [Realtime transcript read in error "limb"] to Brcko, so that is when I found out that these from the TO had been transferred to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we just have one small clarification in transcript on page 85, line 12, it says, "that was when I took him to much Brcko, drove limb to Brcko." So it doesn't make much sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think those are spelling mistakes. I'm sure when they have the audio, they will correct it, or you can correct it, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I heard the witness say that he took him to Brcko, drove him to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So these are just spelling mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's pretty obvious what the mistake is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, so we with proceed, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So when you got to Brcko, where did you take him?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in Brcko we went to the garrison. Mr. Zaric went into the premises of the garrison and I stayed with the duty officer at the Brcko garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How long did Mr. Zaric stay there?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: He stayed there perhaps a half an hour, three-quarters of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And then you went back to Samac?

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: And we went back to Samac again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now I'd like to ask the witness a question regarding an event involving a protected witness so I would ask if we can go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, can we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Here you mentioned that you often took Mr. Zaric to the command of the 17th Tactical Group in Pelagicevo. What did you find out about the crime that happened in Crkvina and how did you find out about that? Can you tell us just, please, slow down, so that the interpreters can follow you.

utterances.speaker: TEODOR TUTNJEVIC
utterances.text: One evening, we went to Pelagicevo, to the command. I drove Simo Zaric there. We stayed there for a while, for a longer time, and on the way back from Pelagicevo, we arrived at the intersection at the village of Crkvina, which is about five kilometres distance from Samac. Approaching the intersection, I saw a few vehicles and I slowed down my driving. At that moment, Sasa Maslic approached me. He recognised our vehicle so I opened the window and he said, "Oh, Uncle Simo, you know what happened last night here?" So Simo said, "what?" And then he answered, "Lugar came and killed 15 or 16 people." I think he said 15. I'm not sure about the number. About the figure. And Simo again said, "what?" And the answer was, "he killed 15 people." "Where did he kill them?" He said, "he killed them here in Crkvina in the warehouse." "Does anyone know about this?" And he said "I don't know. But sometime ago, Mr. Blagoje Simic drove -- went by," and then Simo told me, "come on, let's go to the command of the 2nd battalion, of the 2nd Detachment." That was in Crkvina, in a hamlet. It's a hamlet called Starcevici. So I drove Mr. Zaric there and he went to that command and I stayed outside. He did not stay long. He went out and he went into the car and he said to drive him home.
